landing.metaTitle: ADHD self-report for adults — free screening | NURA
landing.metaDescription: Free adult ADHD self-report using the ASRS-v1.1 scale from the World Health Organization. 18 items, 3 to 5 minutes, no card required. A screening instrument — not a diagnosis.
landing.intro: A structured experience for observing how your attention behaves day to day: where it holds, where it slips, and which patterns repeat. The initial result is free and immediate.
landing.forWhom: For adults who recognise persistent difficulty with focus, organisation or impulse regulation and want to understand those patterns better — out of curiosity, or as a step before a professional assessment.
landing.methodology: This self-report uses the ASRS-v1.1 (Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale), developed by the World Health Organization in partnership with Harvard Medical School. It has 18 items: the first six form Part A, the screening block that flags patterns consistent with ADHD; the remaining twelve detail inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity.
landing.disclaimer: This is a screening and self-knowledge tool. The result is informative, does not constitute a medical diagnosis and does not replace assessment by a qualified professional.

landing.metaTitle: Autism spectrum traits: a self-assessment for adults | NURA
landing.metaDescription: Free self-assessment of spectrum traits in adults. 40 questions on communication, routine, sensory processing and focus. NURA's own scale — not a diagnosis.
landing.lead: 40 questions, 8 to 12 minutes. The initial result is free and arrives at once.
landing.intro: A structured reading of how you communicate, how much routine holds you up, how your senses answer the room, and where your attention goes deep. Not to tell you what you are, but to organise what you already notice in yourself — and give it a name.
landing.forWhom: For adults who recognise themselves in persistent difficulty with social interaction, changes of routine or sensory sensitivity, and want to understand those patterns better — out of curiosity, or as a step before a professional assessment. Many people arrive at this question late, after years of assuming it was shyness, stubbornness or making a fuss.
landing.methodology: This self-assessment uses the NURA spectrum traits scale: 40 items written by us and organised into four territories the literature describes — social communication, routine and repetition, sensory processing, and focus and detail. Six items are written in the opposite direction, so that agreeing with everything out of habit does not produce a high score that means nothing. Unlike the ADHD assessment, which uses the World Health Organization's ASRS-v1.1, this scale is our own and has not been through a validation study — it organises a self-observation, and that is how it should be read.
landing.limits: It is not a diagnostic instrument and has no clinical cut-off. Spectrum traits appear to different degrees across the whole population, and recognising several of them in yourself does not mean having a diagnosis — just as recognising few does not rule one out. Anxiety, ADHD, trauma and personality traits produce similar patterns on some of these questions. Confirmation requires assessment by a psychologist or psychiatrist experienced in adult autism.
landing.disclaimer: A self-knowledge tool. The result is informative, is not a diagnosis and does not replace assessment by a qualified professional.

landing.metaTitle: Online IQ test — 45-question reasoning assessment | NURA
landing.metaDescription: A reasoning assessment with 45 questions across six cognitive dimensions: patterns, logic, matrices, spatial orientation, visual perception and working memory. Immediate result.
landing.lead: Forty-five questions of increasing difficulty, timed. You get a profile per dimension, not just a number.
landing.intro: Most online IQ tests hand back a number and nothing else. This one hands back where your reasoning holds and where it slips — because knowing you do better on patterns than on mental rotation is more useful than any score on its own.
landing.forWhom: For anyone curious about how their own thinking works who wants something more consistent than a social-media quiz. It serves as self-knowledge and as a starting point — not as a clinical assessment, and not as grounds for a career or study decision.
landing.methodology: Forty-five original items, written for NURA, across six dimensions: pattern recognition, analytical thinking, abstract reasoning, spatial orientation, visual perception and working memory. Difficulty rises through the test, and each correct answer is weighted by how hard the item is. Total time is recorded and shifts the result slightly — being right counts for far more than being fast.
landing.limits: This test does not produce an IQ. An IQ score is a normalised position within a standardisation sample, controlled for age and education, administered by a qualified professional — none of which exists here. What you get is a score on NURA's own scale and a performance profile by dimension. It is not for diagnosis, does not measure intelligence in full, and does not replace psychological assessment.
landing.disclaimer: A reasoning assessment for self-knowledge. It is not a psychological test, a diagnosis or a professional opinion.

report.title: Your attention patterns, in detail
report.lead: This report was built from the answers you gave. It organises what came up and explains what each pattern tends to mean day to day.
report.itemsLabel: Items you answered in the clinically relevant range:
report.disclaimer: This report interprets answers to a screening instrument (ASRS-v1.1, World Health Organization). It is informative, is not a diagnosis and does not replace assessment by a qualified professional.

s1.elevated: You marked {count} of the 6 Part A items in the range the instrument treats as relevant. The cutoff is {cutoff}. Your answers fall in the range the scale describes as highly consistent with ADHD — a signal that it is worth investigating, not a conclusion. Screening identifies who should be assessed; it does not assess. That distinction matters: some people in this range receive a different diagnosis in the end, and some receive none.
s1.notElevated: You marked {count} of the 6 Part A items in the relevant range, below the cutoff of {cutoff}. By the scale's criterion, no elevated pattern appeared. This does not rule ADHD out: screening tools are built to err towards finding rather than missing, and cases still slip through — especially in people who developed coping strategies over the years.

s2.some: Of the 9 items linked to inattention, {flagged} appeared in your answers. These items cover sustaining focus on long tasks, organising steps, remembering commitments and finishing what was started. When several appear together, they often describe someone who begins well and loses traction midway — not from lack of interest, but because holding attention on something that is no longer new takes an effort not everyone has to make.
s2.none: None of the 9 items linked to inattention appeared in the relevant range. Sustaining focus, organising and finishing tasks did not stand out as difficulties in your answers.

s3.some: Of the 9 items linked to hyperactivity and impulsivity, {flagged} appeared. These cover restlessness, difficulty settling, talking too much, interrupting and acting before thinking. In adults this rarely looks like the visible agitation of childhood — it tends to show up as internal restlessness, difficulty relaxing even at rest, or decisions made too fast.
s3.none: None of the 9 items linked to hyperactivity and impulsivity appeared in the relevant range. Restlessness and impulsivity did not stand out in your answers.

s4.inattentionHigher: Your answers concentrated more items in inattention ({inattention}) than in hyperactivity and impulsivity ({hyperactivity}). This describes the shape of what you answered, not a type. Profiles like this tend to go unnoticed for longer, because the difficulty reads as forgetfulness or disorganisation — things often taken for carelessness rather than signal.
s4.hyperactivityHigher: Your answers concentrated more items in hyperactivity and impulsivity ({hyperactivity}) than in inattention ({inattention}). This describes the shape of what you answered, not a type. Restlessness and impulsivity tend to be noticed earlier by the people around someone than by the person themselves.
s4.similar: Your answers were balanced across both dimensions — {inattention} inattention items and {hyperactivity} hyperactivity and impulsivity items. A profile showing on both fronts tends to be recognised sooner by people nearby, because it affects both organisation and pace.
s4.fewFlags: Neither dimension concentrated items in the relevant range. Your answers describe someone whose attention and pace difficulties did not stand out on this instrument.

s5.noSetting: Attention patterns show up differently depending on the setting. At work they tend to appear as deadlines and meetings; in study, as difficulty resuming after interruptions; in personal routine, as tasks that pile up. Noticing where the difficulty bites hardest helps describe the situation at an appointment.

setting.work: You said difficulty shows up most at work. There the patterns tend to appear as slipping deadlines, meetings that demand sustained attention and admin tasks that accumulate. It is worth noticing whether new work differs from repetitive work — the gap between the two is often revealing.
setting.study: You said difficulty shows up most in your studies. Here the patterns tend to appear at the moment of starting, in difficulty resuming after an interruption, and in reading that has to be done twice. Notice how much time passes between sitting down and actually beginning.
setting.home: You said difficulty shows up most in your personal routine. In this context patterns appear as household tasks piling up, forgotten bills and plans that never move. It is the setting with the least external structure, which is why difficulty is often most visible there.
setting.several: You reported difficulty across several settings. That is relevant: one of the criteria a professional investigates is precisely whether signs appear in more than one environment rather than in a single situation. Worth mentioning explicitly at an appointment.

since.childhood: You said you have noticed these patterns since childhood. This is usually asked early in an assessment.
since.adolescence: You said you have noticed these patterns since adolescence. It is worth trying to recall earlier situations — childhood is the period an assessment tends to investigate.
since.adulthood: You said you noticed these patterns in adulthood. Worth exploring whether they existed earlier in a less visible form, when there was more external structure.
since.recent: You said you have noticed these patterns only recently. Recent changes deserve attention: poor sleep, prolonged stress, anxiety and depression produce similar symptoms and are investigated alongside.
since.unsure: You said you are not sure how long you have noticed these patterns. That is fine — reconstructing that timeline is part of an assessment's work, not a prerequisite for seeking one.

s6.elevated: If you decide to see a professional — a psychiatrist, neurologist or psychologist experienced in adult ADHD — take this report. It does not replace the assessment, but it saves appointment time. A professional will investigate what a questionnaire cannot reach: when the signs began, how many settings they appear in, how much they actually interfere, and what else could explain them. Come prepared to talk about concrete, recent examples rather than general impressions.
s6.notElevated: If the signs keep bothering you day to day, seeing a professional still makes sense, even with this result. A screening below the cutoff does not close the question — it only means this particular instrument did not find the pattern. Anxiety, depression, sleep deprivation and prolonged stress produce similar symptoms and deserve investigation of their own.

q1.corpo: Before any number: this is not an IQ. The score you are about to see is NURA's own scale, calibrated for this set of 45 questions — it describes how you did on this test, on this day. A real IQ comes from a standardised instrument, administered and interpreted by a qualified professional, with history and clinical observation. None of that fits in an online test, and promising otherwise would be selling an answer nobody can give here.
q1.nota: What this report does well is something else, and it has value: showing the shape of your reasoning. Where it is fast, where it is careful, where it needs more passes. You recognise that in daily life — and it is what you can actually use.

q2.acima: You scored {pontos} points, with {acertos} correct out of {total} questions. That sits above the middle of the scale. Worth understanding what the number already accounts for: questions are not worth the same. They grow harder through the test, and getting the later ones right weighs more than the early ones. Two people with the same number correct can end with different scores, and the difference is which questions each of them solved.
q2.centro: You scored {pontos} points, with {acertos} correct out of {total} questions — near the middle of the scale. Worth understanding what the number already accounts for: questions are not worth the same. They grow harder through the test, and getting the later ones right weighs more than the early ones. Two people with the same number correct can end with different scores, and the difference is which questions each of them solved.
q2.abaixo: You scored {pontos} points, with {acertos} correct out of {total} questions. Before drawing a conclusion, two things: the questions grow harder, so missing the later ones is expected and weighs less than it seems. And a single test measures a day — sleep, hurry, surroundings and mood enter the result without asking. What is low here does not describe a limit of yours; it describes this session.

q3.lead: The 45 questions split into six kinds of reasoning. Each bar is your accuracy within that group.
q3.parelho: Your profile is even: {amplitude} percentage points separate the highest dimension from the lowest. That describes someone who applies a similar way of thinking to problems of different natures — consistent, with no preferred way in. The advantage is not stalling on a specific kind of problem; the cost is having no natural shortcut into any of them.
q3.misto: Your profile has relief: {amplitude} percentage points separate the highest dimension from the lowest. This is the most common shape, and a good sign the test caught real difference rather than noise. You have ground where you think with more room and ground where you need more passes — which describes preference, not ceiling.
q3.irregular: Your profile is quite uneven: {amplitude} percentage points separate the highest dimension from the lowest. Profiles like this usually point to a marked way of thinking — someone who solves very well by one route and avoids another. That can be concentrated talent, but it can also be a block of questions that caught you at a bad moment in the test. Worth noticing which of the two explanations matches your experience.

q4.doisEixos: Your best results came from {forte1} and {forte2}. The lowest, from {fraco1} and {fraco2}. Before treating that as a portrait of your reasoning, check one thing: the questions appear in growing difficulty and interleaved by type, so a dimension may have come out low because its items landed near the end, when fatigue was already weighing. If the low result here matches what you already notice in yourself, it is probably real. If it surprised you, doubt the test before doubting yourself.
q4.umEixo: The test did not separate strong and weak dimensions clearly enough to highlight two of each — your results came out too close to one another. That happens and is not a failure: it means you answered similarly across different natures of problem.

q5.lead: Time alone says nothing. What says something is where time meets accuracy.
q5.rapidoPreciso: You finished in {minutos} minutes — below the {referencia} of reference — and got {acertos} of {total} right. Fast and correct at once usually points to recognition: you see the structure of a problem before solving it step by step. That is a real advantage, and it has a blind spot — problems that look familiar but are not slip through precisely because the answer came too easily.
q5.rapidoImpreciso: You finished in {minutos} minutes — below the {referencia} of reference — with {acertos} correct out of {total}. The combination suggests deciding too early: you reach a plausible answer and move on, without the second look that would separate the plausible from the correct. It is the easiest pattern in this whole report to change. On questions like these, make yourself check the second most likely option before answering.
q5.lentoPreciso: You took {minutos} minutes — above the {referencia} of reference — and got {acertos} of {total} right. That describes care: you check before answering, and the number correct shows the care pays off. The cost appears when a clock is running — an exam, an interview, a short deadline — because the same method that gives you accuracy consumes the time you will not have.
q5.lentoImpreciso: You took {minutos} minutes — above the {referencia} of reference — with {acertos} correct out of {total}. High time with low accuracy is usually not a lack of capacity: it is friction. It may have been fatigue, interruption, a noisy environment, or questions of a kind that demand more passes from you than usual. If you can, take it again on another day, rested and uninterrupted, and compare. The difference between the two sessions says more than either one alone.

q6.corpo: This test measures reasoning in closed situations, with one right answer and no context. It does not measure creativity, judgement, the ability to work with other people, persistence in the face of a problem with no known solution, or accumulated knowledge — which are the things that most decide what someone builds in life.
q6.nota: Take this as a photograph from one angle, not as a portrait. If a result surprised you, the most useful question is not whether you are like that, but where, in your day, you have already seen it happen.

iq_report.noPercentile: This report carries no comparison with other people. A percentile only means something when there is a base of people measured under the same conditions to compare against, and NURA is still gathering that base. We would rather show nothing than show an invented number — when the base exists, it appears here and says how many people you are being compared with.

dimensionMeans.reconhecimento_padroes: Spotting the rule that organises a sequence and predicting what comes next.
dimensionMeans.pensamento_analitico: Breaking a problem into parts and reaching the conclusion the parts support.
dimensionMeans.raciocinio_abstrato: Working with relations that do not depend on concrete content — form, analogy, transformation.
dimensionMeans.orientacao_espacial: Rotating, folding and repositioning objects mentally, without drawing them.
dimensionMeans.percepcao_visual: Noticing difference, detail and visual organisation under time pressure.
dimensionMeans.memoria_trabalho: Holding information in mind while doing something else with it.

reconhecimento_padroes.alto: You read structure quickly. Where a rule hides inside a sequence, you tend to find it — which helps with anything that repeats with variation, from a spreadsheet to a work routine.
reconhecimento_padroes.medio: You find the rule when it is reasonably visible, and need more time when the sequence mixes more than one criterion at once.
reconhecimento_padroes.baixo: Sequences were the hardest ground here. Worth noticing whether the obstacle was seeing the rule or holding it to the end — they are different things, and the second improves with practice.

pensamento_analitico.alto: You follow a chain of premises without losing your place. It is the ability behind argument, diagnosis and any decision where the conclusion must come from the parts and not from impression.
pensamento_analitico.medio: You reach the conclusion when the steps are few, and the path gets costlier when the problem asks you to hold three or four conditions at once.
pensamento_analitico.baixo: Deduction questions cost you the most. Often that is less about logic and more about load: too much information at once. Writing the premises down instead of holding them in your head usually changes this result a lot.

raciocinio_abstrato.alto: You work well far from the concrete — analogies, transformations, relations between shapes with no meaning of their own. It is the kind of reasoning that lets you carry a solution from one domain to another.
raciocinio_abstrato.medio: You follow abstraction when there is some concrete support, and find it harder when the problem is purely relational.
raciocinio_abstrato.baixo: This was one of the hardest grounds. Abstract reasoning is also the most sensitive to fatigue of them all, because there is no context to support memory — worth noticing where in the test those questions reached you.

orientacao_espacial.alto: You rotate and fold objects mentally with ease. It is a concrete and quite specific ability — it shows up in reading plans, assembly, navigation and anything in three dimensions.
orientacao_espacial.medio: You solve simple rotations and need more time when there is more than one chained movement, like rotating and then mirroring.
orientacao_espacial.baixo: Spatial questions slipped away the most. It is the dimension with the widest differences between people, and also the one that responds most to training — those who draw, build or play with space improve measurably.

percepcao_visual.alto: You notice detail and difference quickly, without scanning everything. It helps with reviewing, checking, and any work where the error is in plain sight but goes unnoticed.
percepcao_visual.medio: You catch differences when they are of size or position, and take longer when the difference is in orientation or in a small detail.
percepcao_visual.baixo: Perception questions were the hardest. Worth telling apart two quite different causes: not seeing the detail, or seeing it and not trusting it. The second improves only through the habit of answering on first impression.

memoria_trabalho.alto: You hold information while operating on it — which supports mental arithmetic, following a long conversation and not losing the thread when interrupted.
memoria_trabalho.medio: You hold short sequences well and feel the difference when they grow or when something happens in between.
memoria_trabalho.baixo: Memory questions cost you the most. This is the result in the whole test most sensitive to sleep, anxiety and interruption — before reading it as a trait of yours, worth checking the conditions you answered in.

iq_report.closing: If a result caught your attention, the most useful step is not repeating the test until the number goes up. It is watching where, in your week, that shows up — and, if it genuinely and persistently gets in the way, taking the observation to a professional. A psychologist trained in cognitive assessment works with instruments this one does not replace.
iq_report.disclaimer: This report is for information and self-knowledge. It is not a diagnosis, not a measure of IQ, and does not replace assessment by a qualified professional.

0.lead: The next questions stay with your daily life. Answer thinking about how things actually are for you, not how you think they should be — the result is only worth anything if it describes you.

1.title: You have answered twenty.
1.lead: From here the questions lean more on senses and routine. If one feels odd or does not apply to you, answer as close to your experience as you can and move on — no single question decides the result.

espectro_result.title: What your answers showed.
espectro_result.noCutoff: This scale has no clinical cut-off. The bands describe; they do not classify.

bandTitle.poucos: You recognised few of these traits in yourself.
bandTitle.alguns: You recognised some of these traits in yourself.
bandTitle.muitos: You recognised many of these traits in yourself.

bandBody.poucos: That describes your answers today, and nothing more. It rules nothing out: plenty of autistic people score low on questionnaires like this, having learned to mask early, not recognising in words what they feel, or because the trait shows up in contexts these questions did not reach. If something still bothers you, a low result here is no reason to stop looking.
bandBody.alguns: Some territories showed up, others did not. This is the most common result, and also the easiest to misread in both directions — it neither confirms nor rules out. What it offers is a map of where to look: the territories that showed up are worth watching in your daily life, and the ones that did not are probably not where your friction is.
bandBody.muitos: Several traits showed up, spread across the territories. This is not a diagnosis and cannot become one on its own — but it is a result that deserves being taken seriously rather than filed away. If these patterns persistently get in the way of your life, it is worth seeking assessment from someone who works with adult autism.

espectro_result.domainsLead: The 40 items split into four territories of ten. Here is how many you recognised in each.

next.poucos: If you took this test because of something concrete that bothers you, a low result does not answer that question — it only says these 40 items did not catch it. It is worth describing to a professional what brought you here, with examples from your day, rather than starting from a label.
next.alguns: Take the territories that showed up into a conversation with a professional, with concrete examples. The useful question is not whether you are on the spectrum, but what explains what you feel and what helps — and those two answers are sometimes independent of the diagnosis.
next.muitos: Look for a psychologist or psychiatrist experienced in adult autism. Diagnosis in adults requires a life history, not a questionnaire: bring examples from childhood, school, work and relationships. If someone has known you since early on, their memory usually counts for a lot in the assessment.

espectro_report.title: The map of your traits.
espectro_report.lead: This report opens up what your 40 answers showed, territory by territory: where traits appeared, where they did not, and what that describes — and what it does not.

sections.s2: Communication: what showed up in your answers
sections.s3: Routine, repetition and what predictability holds up

s1.poucos: You recognised {total} of the {maximo} traits. Before any reading: a low number here rules nothing out, and it matters to understand why. Plenty of autistic people score low on questionnaires like this — having learned to mask early, to the point of no longer recognising the effort as effort; not having the words for what they feel; or because the trait shows up in contexts these 40 questions did not reach. If something still bothers you, this report helps name what, and a low result is no reason to close the question.
s1.alguns: You recognised {total} of the {maximo} traits. It is the most common result, and the easiest to misread in both directions — it neither confirms nor rules out. What it offers is a map: some territories showed up and others did not, and that distribution says more than the total. The pages that follow walk through all four, one at a time.
s1.muitos: You recognised {total} of the {maximo} traits. It is a result that deserves being taken seriously, and that is exactly why it needs reading carefully: it is not a diagnosis and cannot become one on its own. Diagnosing autism in adults requires life history, observation and a trained professional — a questionnaire answered in twelve minutes does not reach that, however good it is. What this report does is organise what you already notice, so a conversation with a professional starts ahead.

s2.forte: You recognised {reconhecidos} of {total} items in this territory. Communication is where the effort tends to be most invisible to others and most expensive for you: reading what was not said, holding eye contact, noticing when a conversation has ended. Many people describe this as exhaustion after social events that looked easy from outside. If you recognise yourself here, notice how much time alone you need afterwards — that number usually says more about the cost than the interaction itself.
s2.parcial: You recognised {reconhecidos} of {total} items in this territory. Some of communication flows and some of it costs. The friction commonly shows up in specific situations — large groups, new people, conversations with no clear purpose — and disappears in others, with people you know or on a subject you master. Noticing which of the two you were in when you felt bad usually explains more than any single trait.
s2.leve: You recognised {reconhecidos} of {total} items in this territory. Social communication is not where the traits showed up for you. That is useful information, not just absence: if what brought you here was difficulty in relationships, the explanation is probably elsewhere — social anxiety, past experience, or simply preference. Worth looking at the territories that scored higher.

s3.forte: You recognised {reconhecidos} of {total} items in this territory. Routine and predictability hold you up markedly, and breaking them costs more than it tends to cost people around you. This is rarely stubbornness: a stable routine frees attention that, without it, is spent deciding small things all day. The practical point is that planning changes ahead is not fussiness — it is what gives that attention back to what matters.
s3.parcial: You recognised {reconhecidos} of {total} items in this territory. You have structures that hold you up without the whole routine needing to be rigid. Worth noticing which ones specifically: usually there are few, very specific, and it is breaking those — not any plan — that produces the discomfort.
s3.leve: You recognised {reconhecidos} of {total} items in this territory. Routine and repetition are not where the traits showed up. You handle change without it charging a high price, which is real flexibility and not always recognised as such.

s4.forte: You recognised {reconhecidos} of {total} items in this territory. The sensory is where the difference between your experience and that of the person beside you is most concrete and hardest to explain: a sound nobody else hears, a label nobody else feels, a light that only bothers you. It is not exaggeration and not emotional oversensitivity — it is information coming in, and it arrives differently. The most useful practical consequence is that environmental adjustments work: headphones, lower light, chosen fabric. They tend to be the interventions with the greatest effect and the lowest cost.
s4.parcial: You recognised {reconhecidos} of {total} items in this territory. Some channels overload you and others do not. Worth identifying which specifically — sound, light, texture, touch — because the solution differs for each, and trying to fix them all at once usually fixes none.
s4.leve: You recognised {reconhecidos} of {total} items in this territory. Sensory processing is not where the traits showed up. Busy environments, noise and texture are not your main point of friction.

s5.forte: You recognised {reconhecidos} of {total} items in this territory. Your attention goes deep, and pulling it away from where it is costs a lot. That has two sides that come together: it is the same trait that sustains deep knowledge of a subject and makes interruptions disproportionately irritating. Worth organising the day in blocks rather than fighting your own way of focusing — it is more asset than defect when the environment allows it.
s5.parcial: You recognised {reconhecidos} of {total} items in this territory. You go deep on some things and switch focus easily on others. Noticing what the difference is — subject, environment, time of day — usually pays off more than trying to increase focus in general.
s5.leve: You recognised {reconhecidos} of {total} items in this territory. Deep focus and prolonged interest are not where the traits showed up. You move between subjects without the switch charging a price.

s6.concentrado: Your traits are concentrated: {amplitude} items separate the territory that showed up most from the one that showed up least. Profiles like this usually mean the friction in your life has an address — and that is practical good news, because concentrated intervention works better than general adjustment. Worth starting with the highest territory and watching how much of your day's discomfort it explains on its own.
s6.irregular: Your traits have relief: {amplitude} items separate the highest territory from the lowest. This is the most common shape and a good sign the test caught real difference rather than everything being answered alike. You have ground where life charges more and ground where it does not.
s6.espalhado: Your traits are spread evenly: only {amplitude} items separate the highest territory from the lowest. A profile like this describes someone whose experience is consistent across different situations rather than concentrated in one kind. Worth looking less for a single culprit and more at the accumulation across the day.

espectro_report.profileLead: How many items you recognised in each of the four groups of ten.
espectro_report.closingTitle: What to bring and what to ask at an assessment
espectro_report.closing: If you decide to seek an assessment, bring concrete examples and not conclusions. What a professional needs is history: what it was like in childhood, at school, in early relationships; what changed and what never did; where the effort shows up today. If someone has known you since early on — a parent, a sibling, an old friend — their memory usually counts as much as yours, because much of what became automatic was visible from outside when it began. This report works as a starting point for that conversation, not a substitute for it.
espectro_report.limitsTitle: What this test does not reach
espectro_report.limits: This is NURA's own scale, with no validation study: it has no known sensitivity or specificity and does not separate those who have from those who do not. Anxiety, ADHD, trauma and personality traits produce similar patterns on several of these questions. And it measures what you recognise in yourself — which depends on how much you have already thought about the subject, and is exactly why many people score differently before and after talking to a professional.
espectro_report.disclaimer: This report is for information and self-knowledge. It is not a diagnosis, does not replace assessment by a qualified professional, and the scale that produced it has not been through a validation study.
